props.title: Medium Cool
props.initialSlug: Cameraman's ethics clash amid 1968 Chicago riots

sections.content: Medium Cool revolutionized the intersection of documentary and fiction filmmaking. Director Haskell Wexler, an accomplished cinematographer, threw his cameras into the explosive 1968 Democratic Convention protests in Chicago, weaving a fictional story around real unfolding chaos. The film predated the found-footage genre by decades, blending scripted scenes with actual riot footage so seamlessly that when tear gas appears on screen, you hear someone yell "Look out, Haskell - it's real!" This groundbreaking approach influenced later works like The Battle of Algiers (1966) and Z (1969), establishing a new vocabulary for political filmmaking.

sections.content: Wexler's background as a cinematographer for films like Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1966) informed Medium Cool's distinctive visual style. He employed handheld cameras and natural lighting to create an immediate, visceral feeling that became a hallmark of New Hollywood cinema. This approach directly influenced later films like Network (1976) and Dog Day Afternoon (1975), which similarly explored media manipulation and social unrest through a documentary-influenced lens.

The film's examination of media ethics and responsibility remains startlingly relevant. When protagonist John Cassellis questions his role as an objective observer versus an active participant, it anticipates similar themes in films like Nightcrawler (2014) and Natural Born Killers (1994). The way Medium Cool captures the violence and chaos of the 1968 convention presaged how future filmmakers would incorporate real footage into narrative films, from Malcolm X (1992) to BlacKkKlansman (2018). sections.content: Medium Cool's influence extends beyond its technical innovations. The film's fearless mixing of fiction and reality created a template for politically engaged cinema that continues today. Films like Good Night, and Good Luck (2005) and The Trial of the Chicago 7 (2020) follow its example of using historical events as backdrop for dramatic narratives while maintaining journalistic integrity. Wexler's approach to filming actual protests while protecting his actors and crew established safety protocols still used when filming in volatile situations.
